edges.description: Persistent airway infection and higher bacterial burden sustain the characteristic neutrophilic inflammatory response.
Persistent infection, inflammation, and mucus obstruction cause progressive structural airway damage that culminates in irreversible bronchial dilation.
Recurrent increases in infection and inflammation manifest clinically as pulmonary exacerbations.
The chronic disease burden and exacerbation episodes contribute to clinically important fatigue.
Irreversible structural destruction and dilation of the bronchial walls produces the progressive, fixed airflow limitation seen in bronchiectasis.
Airway structural damage and airflow limitation manifest clinically as breathlessness.
Distorted, dilated airways and luminal narrowing during airflow produce wheeze.
Bronchial wall destruction with hypertrophied, fragile bronchial arteries predisposes to airway bleeding.
Distorted, secretion-filled airways generate discontinuous adventitious sounds on auscultation.
Retained sputum creates a reservoir for persistent infection and inflammation, completing the vicious-vortex feedback loop.
Failure to clear mucus and trapped microbes permits persistent and recurrent airway infection.
Retained, hyperconcentrated airway secretions stimulate the cough reflex.
Excessive neutrophil serine protease release overwhelms airway antiproteases, establishing the protease-antiprotease imbalance.
Protease-driven destruction of airway-wall elastin and collagen drives the irreversible bronchial dilation.
Excess neutrophil elastase reduces ciliary beating and thereby weakens effective airway clearance.
Neutrophil elastase induces epithelial MUC5AC expression and promotes mucus hypersecretion and goblet-cell metaplasia.
